title: CIDB Half Marathon 2026 Review: Putrajaya's Community Race at Dataran Putrajaya
seo_title: CIDB Half Marathon 2026 Review: Course, Tips & Registration Guide
meta_description: Comprehensive CIDB Half Marathon 2026 review: December 13 at Dataran Putrajaya. 21K, 10K, 5K, and 3K distances organised by Kelab CIDB. Registration open via Checkpoint Spot. Everything Klang Valley runners need to know.
dek: A community-organised half marathon by Kelab CIDB (the Construction Industry Development Board club) at Dataran Putrajaya — Malaysia's grand administrative capital — on December 13, 2026. With four distances from 21K down to 3K, open registration through Checkpoint Spot, and a course running through one of the most photogenic government precincts in Southeast Asia, this is a low-key race in a high-drama setting.
verdict: The CIDB Half Marathon occupies an interesting niche in the Klang Valley running calendar: it is a community-organised race by Kelab CIDB (the sports and recreation club of Malaysia's Construction Industry Development Board), held at Dataran Putrajaya — one of the most visually striking race venues in the country. The ceremonial square, flanked by the pink-domed Putra Mosque and the Prime Minister's Office, with Putrajaya Lake as a backdrop, provides a start/finish precinct that punches well above the event's modest organisational weight. Four distances are offered (21K, 10K, 5K, 3K), with the 3K serving as a family-friendly entry point that many races lack. Registration is open and handled through Checkpoint Spot, which is a reliable platform. The December 13 date catches Putrajaya in the inter-monsoon period — mornings are warm (24-26°C) with high humidity, but the risk of heavy monsoon rain is lower than in November. The downsides: Kelab CIDB is a recreational club, not a professional race organiser, and expectations for production values should be calibrated accordingly. On-course support, timing accuracy, and route marking are likely to be functional rather than polished. For Klang Valley runners looking for an accessible, affordable race in a genuinely beautiful setting — and who do not mind a community-club production ethos — the CIDB Half Marathon is a solid pick with the added advantage that you can register for it right now. For runners who demand the precision of a professionally produced event, this may feel undercooked.

sections.heading: What Is the CIDB Half Marathon?
paragraphs: The CIDB Half Marathon is a community road race organised by Kelab CIDB WP Kuala Lumpur — the sports and recreation club of the Construction Industry Development Board (CIDB) Malaysia [1]. CIDB is a statutory body under the Ministry of Works responsible for regulating and developing the Malaysian construction industry, and its staff club organises sports events as part of its member-engagement activities — which means this race has an institutional backing that most community races lack, even if the event-production expertise is not at the level of a professional race organiser [1].

The 2026 edition is scheduled for Sunday, December 13, at Dataran Putrajaya, the ceremonial square of Malaysia's federal administrative capital [1]. Four distances are offered: 21.1K (half marathon), 10K, 5K, and 3K [1]. The inclusion of a 3K distance — shorter than the standard 5K — makes the event accessible to families, children, and first-time participants who might be intimidated by a 5K [1].

Registration is currently open through Checkpoint Spot, the Malaysian race registration platform [1]. The fact that registration is open several months before race day is a positive signal — many Malaysian community races announce registration weeks before the event, making planning difficult for runners [1].

sections.heading: Dataran Putrajaya: Malaysia's Most Photogenic Race Venue?
paragraphs: Dataran Putrajaya is the vast ceremonial square at the heart of Putrajaya, Malaysia's purpose-built administrative capital roughly 25 kilometres south of Kuala Lumpur [2]. The square is framed by the Putra Mosque — with its distinctive pink dome and 116-metre minaret — on one side, the Prime Minister's Office (Perdana Putra) on another, and Putrajaya Lake completing the panorama [2]. For a road race start and finish, it is hard to imagine a more dramatic setting in Malaysia outside of the Petronas Twin Towers.

The surrounding road network is purpose-built for ceremonial and governmental use: wide, multi-lane boulevards with smooth asphalt, generous shoulders, and minimal commercial traffic on weekend mornings [2]. The terrain around Putrajaya is predominantly flat to gently undulating, with the lake and the landscaped gardens providing a green, open backdrop [2]. A half-marathon course starting at the Dataran and looping through the Putrajaya boulevards — past the Seri Wawasan Bridge, through the government precinct, and back to the lakefront — would be fast, scenic, and largely free of the traffic conflicts that plague inner-city KL races [2].

For runners, the practical advantages of a Dataran Putrajaya start are significant: ample parking in the surrounding government complexes, pre-race shelter in the covered walkways around the square, clean public toilets (Putrajaya maintains its facilities well), and a post-race spread of food options at the nearby Alamanda Shopping Centre or the Putrajaya lakefront food stalls [2].

sections.heading: December 13: Inter-Monsoon in Putrajaya
paragraphs: December 13 falls in the inter-monsoon period for Peninsular Malaysia — the northeast monsoon has begun but is typically less intense in the Klang Valley in early December than it becomes in late December and January [3]. Mornings are warm (24-26°C) with humidity above 85%, and the risk of afternoon rain and thunderstorms is present but lower than in November [3].

For a half marathon, an early start (5:00-5:30am) would allow most runners to finish before 8:00am, well ahead of any convective afternoon weather [3]. The humidity at dawn will be substantial — runners should expect to sweat profusely from the first kilometre and should plan hydration accordingly [3].

The late-year date avoids the extreme heat of the March-May period and the peak monsoon flooding of November. For Klang Valley runners who train year-round in these conditions, December is a familiar, manageable race window — not fast, but not punishing [3].

sections.heading: Registration, Logistics, and the CIDB Factor
paragraphs: Registration is open through Checkpoint Spot as of this writing — the listing is at checkpointspot.asia/event/cidb-half-marathon-2026 [1]. Malaysian community-race entry fees on Checkpoint Spot typically range from RM 50-90 depending on distance and registration tier — expect this event to fall at the lower end of that range, consistent with its community-club ethos [1].

Race-day logistics: Dataran Putrajaya is accessible via the MEX Highway from KL (approximately 30 minutes from the city centre without traffic) and via the ELITE Expressway from the south [2]. Parking is available in the government-complex car parks surrounding the square. Public transport via the Putrajaya Sentral ERL station followed by a short Grab or bus ride is an option, though early-morning services may be limited on a Sunday [2].

What to expect from a Kelab CIDB-organised event: a community-club production rather than a professional race-company production. Race packets are likely to include a basic event shirt and a finisher's medal. Timing may be gun-time or basic chip timing. Aid stations are likely to offer water and possibly isotonic drinks, but frequency and quality may vary. Route marking may rely on painted arrows and volunteer marshals rather than professional signage. None of this is a criticism — it is simply the reality of a race where the entry fee is calibrated for community participation rather than premium amenities [1].

sections.heading: Should You Run the CIDB Half Marathon?
paragraphs: If you live in the Klang Valley and value a stunning race venue over slick production: yes, register now. Dataran Putrajaya is a genuinely beautiful place to start and finish a race, the flat-to-rolling course is accessible, and the multi-distance format means you can bring the whole family [1]. At community-race pricing, the value proposition is strong [1].

If you are a runner who collects visually distinctive race experiences: Putrajaya in the early morning — with the pink mosque reflecting off the lake and the wide boulevards empty of traffic — is Instagram gold. The race photos alone will justify the entry fee [2].

If you demand professional race production (chip timing, corral starts, precision aid stations): this community-club event may not meet your standards. The organisers are a recreational sports club, not a race-management company, and the production will reflect that [1]. But for the right runner — one who values setting and community over polish — the CIDB Half Marathon is a worthy addition to the calendar [1].
